replying_to: Replying to Self-Supervised Modality-Invariant and Modality-Specific Feature Learning for 3D Objects
display_title: Official Review of Paper323 by Reviewer RY4y

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a multi-modal self-supervised learning (SSL) model to jointly learn both modality-invariant and modality-specific features with contrastive learning. The multi-modal features learned by the proposed paradigm is validated to be useful on different downstream tasks such as recognition and retrieval. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms a good amount of SSL methods and is on-par with supervised learning methods.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

1. The paper is well-motivated and the objective is clear.
2. Overall, the writting is easy to follow. (See abuse of notations below)  
3. The proposed model is compared with a good amount of SOTA and achieves satisfying results.  
4. Although further elaboration and analysis is definitely needed. This proposed multi-modal SSL model has the potential to be used on a lot more tasks and scenarios.

Major Weaknesses:

1. Abuse of notations. 
    1. In Sec 3.1, modality-invariant features should either be expressed in I_i^1, I_i^2, ..., I_i^M, or I_i. Using superscript m is very confusing. Similarly, for modality-specific features, the last superscipt should be M. 
    2. In Sec 3.2, 6th line, last subscript of G should be M rather than m.
    3. A good amount of other erronous mix between M and m in various other expressions.
    4. A good amount of inconsistency b/w using m and M_i to denote each distinct modality 
2. Novelty. The whole ideas of modality-invarient and modality-specific feature learning is basically applying contrastive loss [1] in the inter- and intra-modality manner. The only novel element is the soft orthogonal feature constraint, yet this part is not given enough discussion and analysis. The overall novelty seems weak.
3. I do agree with the design of constraints L_S and L_I. But I am not convinced by the design of L_O. I think the first term of L_O (inter-modal orthogonality) is a reasonable constraint, but the constraints of orthogonality between modal-specific features is not so obvious. 
    
    In my opinion, the modal-specific features need not be orthogonal to each other — the structure of each modality's feature highly depends on the modality itself and the orthigonality seems to be too strict. This may hinder the learning of these features, because I feel that orthogonality with the modality-invariant conponent is enough to guarentee a good learning. Ablation experiments and further analysis is needed to to validate the usefulness of the second term.
    
4. Error in main figure. L_I denotes modality-invarient loss, which indicates that it should be connected with I features. Yet in Figure 2 it is connected with S features.
5. The generalization concerns. Ideally, the learning paradigm should be independent with the choice of backbone feature encoder. I wonder what the results will be if the backbone is changed. For example, what if another commonly used point encoder PointNet [3] or PointNet++ [4] is used as backbones. 
6. Missing details on reproducibility. What is the actual number of hyperparameters alpha, beta, gamma, in the loss function? How and why is the number chosen in the experiments? How to choose the weight of different terms when the method is used in a new scenario where the modalities available are different from the ones used in the paper? Some ablation experiments or at least some discussion is needed.

Minor Weaknesses:

1. I do not understand why random rotation along one axis is an augmentation to point cloud. DGCNN [2] is used in the manuscript to learn the point feature, and the graph stucture should make the model rotation invariant. Please elaborate more.
2. Discription of constraints in the introduction section is incomplete. Maximizing the similarity b/w same objects is not enough, it should also minimize the similarity b/w different objects in the same time. 
3. Inaccurate citations. E.g., SimCLR [1] is an ICML paper but is cited as arxiv paper. Please make sure your citations are all up-to-date.
4. Visualization in Figure 3 is really good. But it's better if authors can include an additional row with the visualization of hidden feaure F. This helps to understand how the features are projected into two different spaces.




[1] Chen, Ting, et al. "A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2020.

[2] Wang, Yue, et al. "Dynamic graph cnn for learning on point clouds." Acm Transactions On Graphics (tog) 38.5 (2019): 1-12.

[3] Qi, Charles R., et al. "Pointnet: Deep learning on point sets for 3d classification and segmentation." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2017.

[4] Qi, Charles Ruizhongtai, et al. "PointNet++: Deep Hierarchical Feature Learning on Point Sets in a Metric Space." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (2017).
content.summary_of_the_review:
The pros and cons of the paper is discussed in the Main Review. I think this work has the potential to be accepted. However, the current version of the manuscipt is very incomplete. 

Thus, I give it a 3 at this point.

I suggest the authors revise, and add missing part of the paper. I will increase my score if my concerns are resolved later.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper323 by Reviewer RY4y

content.title: Response to Reviewer RY4y
content.comment:
Thanks for  your positive feedback about our idea of multimodal self-supervised feature learning and the extensive experiments. We addressed your great questions and suggestions as follows:

1. Abuse of notations and other issues with the paper writing. 

Response: Thanks for pointing it out. We revised the paper and fixed all the issues.

2. Novelty of the modality-invariant and modality-specific feature learning. The orthogonality with the modality-invariant component is enough to guarantee a good learning. Ablation experiments and further analysis is needed to to validate the usefulness of the second term.

Response: The main novelty of this paper is to jointly learn modality-invariant and modality-specific features from unlabeled multimodal dataset with our proposed constraints. The two constraints can be enforced by any self-supervised metric learning losses such as SimCLR, SimSiam, BYOL, ec. As long as the loss can help to reduce the intra-class variations of the features and increase the inter class variations without using any labels. With extensive experiments and ablation studies, we demonstrated that our proposed three constrains are very effective and outperforms the existing state-of-the-art models by a large margin on some downstream tasks. Our novelty mainly lies in the self-supervised metric features learning rather than the loss of innovation.  From a self-supervised metric learning perspective, we believe that our proposed learning paradigm and the state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks can be regarded as novel. The goal of the orthogonal loss is to enforce the relationship among all the modality-specific features and modality-invariant features. To make sure there are no unnecessary and redundant feature be captured through the self-supervised learning process, we enforce the orthogonality among all these two sets of features. We are working on providing more experimental results for this loss term. 

3. Error in main figure. L_I denotes modality-invarient loss, which indicates that it should be connected with I features. Yet in Figure 2 it is connected with S features.

Response: Thanks for pointing out. We fixed the issue in the main figure and revised the entire paper accordingly. 

4. The generalization concerns. Ideally, the learning paradigm should be independent with the choice of backbone feature encoder. I wonder what the results will be if the backbone is changed. For example, what if another commonly used point encoder PointNet [3] or PointNet++ [4] is used as backbones.

Response: Thanks for the suggestions. We are working on the experiments with different backbones. 

5. Missing details on reproducibility. What is the actual number of hyperparameters alpha, beta, gamma, in the loss function? How and why is the number chosen in the experiments? How to choose the weight of different terms when the method is used in a new scenario where the modalities available are different from the ones used in the paper? Some ablation experiments or at least some discussion is needed.

Response: The weight for each loss term is chosen by ablation studies. We further tuned the hyper-parameters, and found that  3, 2, 1 works best for the invariant loss, specific loss, and orthogonal loss. We are conducting more ablation studies about the hyper-parameters. 

6. I do not understand why random rotation along one axis is an augmentation to point cloud. DGCNN [2] is used in the manuscript to learn the point feature, and the graph stucture should make the model rotation invariant. Please elaborate more.

Response: The data augmentation generates more training samples with slight variations to help reduce the over-fitting. For the data augmentation strategies, we are following the augmentation techniques used in other papers such as DGCNN.  Although the network (DGCNN) itself can handle variations with graph structure, more dataset still can make the model learn more robust features and perform better.

7. Description of constraints in the introduction section is incomplete. Maximizing the similarity b/w same objects is not enough, it should also minimize the similarity b/w different objects at the same time.

Response: We conducted experiments to enforce the modality-invariant and modality-specific constraints by using SimCLR and SimSiam. The performances are comparable when using the two losses. This demonstrates that our model also works with loss that does not specifically minimize the similarity between different objects.

display_title: Official Review of Paper323 by Reviewer wWUD

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper attempts to address the self-supervised learning task for 3D feature learning by proposing to jointly learn features from multiple modalities, such as image, point cloud, and mesh. The proposed method aims to learn two types of features, including modality-invariant features and modality-specific features. The network is trained with the contrastive losses and orthogonality constraints. The learned modality-invariant features can be applied to cross-model retrieval, while the learned modality-specific features can be applied to 3d recognition.

The authors evaluate the performance on ModelNet40 and ModelNet10 dataset for classification and model retrieval.
content.main_review:
STRENGTHS:

- Although there are some works studying the self-supervised problem for 3D feature representations, the proposed method considering the multiple modalities is interesting.
- The method is introduced clearly and easy to understand, in general.
- The provided qualitative visualization in Figure 3 is helpful for readers to understand the method.
- In most cases, the performance improvements can demonstrate the effectiveness.

WEAKNESS:

- Why the cross-view invariant constraint, i.e., Eq. 6, can enforce the network to learn modality-specific features? I am not an expert in contrastive learning. It would be better if the authors can give an explanation.
- For other self-supervised learning methods in Table 1, the SVM is used for classification? I find that several methods, like Orientation, ContextPred, and XMV, perform better than the proposed method only with Point (89.7\%). The authors should give an analysis.
- It would be better if the authors can conduct experiments on other datasets. For example, the authors can fine-tune the pre-trained network on ShapeNet for model retrieval or directly train the model on ShapeNet. Only conducting experiments on ModelNet40 / ModelNet10 is not enough.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is interesting. However, some claims are needed to be clarified, and more experiments are expected.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper323 by Reviewer wWUD

content.title: Response to Reviewer wWUD
content.comment:
Thank you for your positive and constructive feedback about our idea of multimodal self-supervised feature learning. We addressed your great questions and suggestions as follows:

1. Why the cross-view invariant constraint, i.e., Eq. 6, can enforce the network to learn modality-specific features? I am not an expert in contrastive learning. It would be better if the authors can give an explanation.

Response: The basic principle of contrastive learning is to learn representations by contrasting positive and negative pairs. By maximizing the similarity between an anchor sample and a positive sample while minimizing similarity to all other (negative) samples, the meaningful semantic features can be learned through this process. Although without using any labels, the Eq. 6 will eventually encourage the distance of features of objects from the same semantic class are closer, while the distance of features of objects from different class are further. The Eq.6 is enforced over the features for each modality, and the relationship of the features between the two different modalities are not considered with this Equation. Jointly learned with orthogonal constraints, the features learned with Equation 5 and 6 will be modality-specific. 

2. For other self-supervised learning methods in Table 1, the SVM is used for classification? I find that several methods, like Orientation, ContextPred, and XMV, perform better than the proposed method only with Point (89.7%). The authors should give an analysis.

Response: It is a common practice to use SVM over the features extracted from self-supervised learned models. Following the state-of-the-art methods, we also use SVM to get the classification results. We further tuned the hyper-parameters of our model including the weight of the loss and the number of training iterations, and our most recent results are almost the same as the Orientation and ContextPred. The fusion of multimodal features of our model are still significantly higher than these state-of-the-art methods. 

3. It would be better if the authors can conduct experiments on other datasets. For example, the authors can fine-tune the pre-trained network on ShapeNet for model retrieval or directly train the model on ShapeNet. Only conducting experiments on ModelNet40 / ModelNet10 is not enough.

Response: Thanks for the suggestions, we are working on the experiments to transfer the model trained on ShapeNet to ModelNet40/10 datasets.

replying_to: Replying to Self-Supervised Modality-Invariant and Modality-Specific Feature Learning for 3D Objects
display_title: Official Review of Paper323 by Reviewer 6XzF

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to jointly learn features from different modalities including image, point cloud, and mesh in a self-supervised model. To this end, it learns two types of features: modality-invariant features and modality-specific features and enforces a soft orthogonality constraint between the modality-invariant features and modality-specific features. This high-level idea is novel and interesting to the best of my knowledge. The method is validated on ModelNet benchmarks for various retrieval problems.
content.main_review:
My main concern with the paper is the lack of novelty in the contrastive learning pipeline. the contrastive losses are not really novel although I agree the idea of learning modality invariant and specific features on these 3 modalities is new and interesting. However, given that Jing et al. already does cross-modal learning between PC and images, this paper adds another modality of a mesh but it is not fully explored. e.g. Mesh structure brings 3d connectivity information that is absent from PC and images. So one way to incorporate and justify adding another modality would be by enforcing features to learn this extra connectivity information in some way. e.g. by exploiting the Laplacian operator on meshes. 

To summarize, compared to the baseline Jing et al. 2020, the proposed pipeline aims to exploit one more modality of mesh. However, I do not see a direct connection either in loss function or in results. Modelnet is already a saturated benchmark where methods based on just pc already achieve comparable performance.
content.summary_of_the_review: To summarise, I like the high-level idea of learning modality invariant and modality-specific features over images, point cloud, and mesh. However, the methodology lacks novelty from a contrastive learning perspective (e.g. Jing et al. 2020) and empirical advancements do not seem significant as they are limited to only Modelnet with a comparable performance from baselines of 2020. If the authors can justify how/why mesh connectivity is beneficial in the current framework e.g. by providing additional results, I am happy to revisit my score.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper323 by Reviewer 6XzF

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6XzF
content.comment:
​​Thank you for acknowledging that our idea about jointly learning modality-invariant and modality-specific features are new and interesting. You brought up some great questions/suggestions. The following are our responses regarding the questions.

1. The contrastive losses are not really novel although I agree the idea of learning modality invariant and specific features on these 3 modalities is new and interesting. 

Response: The key novelty of this paper is to jointly learn modality-invariant and modality-specific features from unlabeled multimodal dataset. The previous state-of-the-art mainly only focuses on learning discriminate features for point cloud data, while we propose to use the cross-modal correspondence among multi-modalities of data for self-supervised learning. Through extensive experiments, we showed that our proposed three constraints can indeed learn modality-invariant and modality-specific features and our model can significantly outperform the state-of-the-art model on multiple benchmarks. Our novelty mainly lies in the self-supervised metric features learning rather than the loss of innovation. Moreover, the three constraints in our model are carefully designed to learn the features with desired properties and not just simply apply the contrastive loss on a new dataset. The contrastive loss is just a tool to enforce our proposed constraints and our proposed model also works with other losses. We are working on the experiments of our model but using other losses for the proposed modality-invariant and modality-specific constraints. 

2. However, given that XTM already does cross-modal learning between PC and images, this paper adds another modality of a mesh but it is not fully explored. e.g. Mesh structure brings 3d connectivity information that is absent from PC and images.

Response: Although XTM use the relation between the point cloud and multi-view image for self-supervised learning, but the performance are unsatisfactory, i.e. it has low performance for the within-modal retrieval task, the features learned for point cloud and images are in different spaces making the cross-modal retrieval tasks impossible. Compared to XMV (proposed by Jing et al), our classification results of the point cloud modality is 0.8% higher than the results in XMV, while our model outperforms it for the within-domain retrieval task by more than 30%. Moreover, our model is able to learn modality-invariant features which can be used for cross-modal retrieval tasks, while XMV is not able to learn modality-invariant features. 

Our model is significantly different from XMV while our model performs much better than XMV. XMV only learns features without any constraints for two modalities, while our model learns two types of features including modality-invariant and modality-specific. XMV cannot be used for cross-modal retrieval tasks, while the features learned by our model achieves high performance for both within-modal and cross-modal retrieval.

3. So one way to incorporate and justify adding another modality would be by enforcing features to learn this extra connectivity information in some way. e.g. by exploiting the Laplacian operator on meshes. 

Response: In this paper, we mainly focus on learning the relationship between the features of different modalities, i.e. the features between the point cloud, mesh, image. We do not specifically focus on the detailed structure of any of the modalities. The key reason is that we want to learn high-level features with certain relationships, i.e. modality-invariant features, modality-specific features, and the orthogonal relationship. Focusing on the structure of each modality is out of the scope of this paper.

4. More results on other datasets. 

Response. Thanks for the suggestions. We are working on the experiments on other datasets.
